target: AG1's claim that a national Election Day holiday would reliably free people to vote by removing the scheduling barrier caused by work and school.
objection: A federal holiday would not require private employers to give paid time off, so many low-income workers in retail, food service, and gig work could still have to work or lose wages; therefore the holiday would not reliably remove the barrier for the people most constrained.

target: AG1's assumption that a holiday is an effective turnout strategy on its own.
objection: Research and policy comparisons suggest that making Election Day a holiday by itself is not a proven or especially effective way to increase turnout, especially compared with more direct voting-access reforms such as employer time-to-vote rules, early/absentee/mail voting, reduced registration friction, and automatic voter registration.

target: AG2's argument that a holiday still won't guarantee paid time off and that other reforms are more evidence-aligned.
objection: Even without a paid-leave mandate, federal holidays change real-world logistics: more businesses close or reduce hours, public institutions and childcare arrangements are more available, and employers are less likely to force employees to choose between wages and voting, so the holiday can still reduce scheduling barriers.

target: AG1's claim that holiday-related logistics changes will reliably help low-income workers.
objection: Even on holidays, retail, service, and other low-wage jobs frequently remain open with essential staffing, so those workers may still be scheduled to work and face the same wages-versus-voting tradeoff; the holiday does not reliably translate into lost-wage protection.

target: AG1's assumption that a holiday reduces the need to request time off and therefore helps low-income workers.
objection: For low-income workers, the main bottleneck is not convenience but whether they can vote without losing income, and a holiday without mandatory paid time to vote can widen inequality by helping more flexible workers while retail/service workers still work or take unpaid time.

target: AG1's suggestion that a holiday can simply be added alongside other reforms without problem.
objection: Calling the holiday an add-on does not answer the policy question, because by itself it is still an unreliable way to fix the real constraint; the direct employer-facing reforms are the dependable fix and should be prioritized instead of relying on a federally declared day off.

target: AG2's claim that if time-to-vote protections are needed, a holiday is an extra costly layer rather than the main solution.
objection: A holiday and time-to-vote protections address different parts of the problem: the holiday reduces how much time people need by changing the surrounding work/school schedule, while time-to-vote rules protect wages; they are not redundant.

target: AG2's claim that a holiday can be treated as an extra layer that is unnecessary once time-to-vote protections exist.
objection: The holiday sets a common nationwide public baseline that changes institutions beyond a single employer, and because time-to-vote rules vary in strength and enforcement, a uniform national holiday still has independent value in reducing scheduling friction.

target: AG1's claim that a holiday and time-to-vote rules are complementary.
objection: If the policy still needs enforceable time-to-vote protections to solve the wage-loss problem, then the holiday is not the solution; it becomes an unnecessary, costly, and uncertain layer that distracts from the direct remedy.

target: AG1's assumption that the holiday meaningfully reduces scheduling conflicts in a way that matters for low-income workers.
objection: Without employer-facing time-to-vote requirements, a federal holiday does not reliably stop private employers from scheduling workers to cover Election Day, so it still fails to protect the workers most at risk of losing income.

target: AG2's claim that a holiday may be an extra costly layer and that the real solution should be direct employer rules.
objection: A holiday and time-to-vote rules are not redundant because they reduce the problem in different ways: the holiday changes the calendar and surrounding routines, while time-to-vote rules address wages; the holiday also gives a common nationwide baseline that is uniform across institutions.

target: AG2's concern that a holiday creates a misallocated fix that diverts political effort away from stronger reforms.
objection: The holiday does not have to replace targeted reforms; it can be pursued alongside them, so the claim that it will necessarily crowd out the other work does not follow.

target: AG2's claim that a holiday is a misallocated fix because it lets policymakers focus on a symbolic calendar change while leaving the real constraint to patchy state rules.
objection: Because the holiday changes the baseline across work, school, childcare, and daytime logistics, it reduces dependence on varied state rules and makes Election Day less likely to become a standard-schedule gotcha.

target: AG1's assumption that changing the day’s surrounding routines is purely beneficial for low-income families.
objection: For many low-income parents, if schools or daycare close but employers still require coverage, the holiday can add new costs—such as emergency childcare or other expenses—without providing paid leave or childcare subsidies, so it can worsen the burdens they already face.

target: AG1's claim that the holiday is additive rather than replacing other reforms.
objection: Politically, once Election Day becomes a holiday, lawmakers and employers may treat the problem as solved and stop pursuing the enforceable wage-protection and access reforms that actually matter, so the additive framing is too optimistic.

target: AG1's claim that adding a holiday and time-to-vote protections together solves the problem.
objection: That concession shows that a holiday alone is not a reliable or equitable solution; if time-to-vote protections must be added to make the policy fair, then the real mechanism is the protections, not the holiday.

target: AG1's broader claim that a federal holiday is the right lever for turnout and access.
objection: Passing a national holiday would require major federal legislation and political capital, which could crowd out faster, more enforceable state or local reforms such as employer time-to-vote requirements and automatic or low-friction registration; the holiday is therefore a lower-leverage path.

target: AG2's claim that a holiday is mostly duplicative once time-to-vote protections exist and that it adds political cost.
objection: A holiday can be bundled with enforceable time-to-vote protections in the same legislation, so the policy need not be either/or; bundling lets government remove the scheduling barrier and prevent wage loss at the same time.

target: AG2's marginal-benefit objection to a national holiday.
objection: A nationwide holiday gives families and workers a clear, predictable calendar baseline well in advance, which helps them plan childcare, transportation, and voting logistics without relying on uncertain employer requests or patchy local rules.

target: AG1's claim that bundling a holiday with time-to-vote rules makes the holiday worthwhile.
objection: If the enforceable time-to-vote rules are doing the heavy lifting to prevent wage loss, then the holiday is mostly duplicative; it adds costs and political tradeoffs without reliably fixing the decisive constraint.

target: AG1's claim that a federal holiday has independent value beyond wage protections.
objection: Because the holiday does not directly address whether workers can take time without losing pay, state-level time-to-vote protections and other direct access reforms are more likely to deliver the real benefit, making the holiday only an uncertain add-on.
